Anthropology

Difference between anthropology and sociology, explained

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

Anthropology studies humans as a whole, across time and cultures, including biology, archaeology and language, and is known for long-term fieldwork in a single community. Sociology studies modern societies and social institutions, often using surveys and statistics. The two share many topics, and in India the boundary between social anthropology and sociology is especially thin.

We run an oral history lab and research methods workshops that give anthropology and sociology students real fieldwork practice, online or on campus.

The short answer

Both subjects study human social life, so the overlap is large. The main differences are in scope and method. Anthropology takes the whole human species as its subject: our evolution, our bodies, our past societies, our languages and our cultures. Sociology concentrates on society, especially modern and industrial society, and on institutions such as the family, education, religion, the economy and the state.

Method is the clearer dividing line. Anthropologists are known for ethnography: living in one place for a long time and learning from the inside. Sociologists use a wider range of tools, including large surveys, census data, statistical models and interviews, alongside ethnography. Neither method belongs exclusively to one subject, but the emphasis is different.

Anthropology and sociology compared

The table below sets out the usual differences. Treat it as a guide to emphasis rather than strict rules, since individual scholars cross these lines all the time.

PointAnthropologySociology
ScopeHumans as a whole: biology, past, language and cultureSociety and social institutions, mostly in the present
Time depthFrom human evolution and prehistory to todayMainly modern and contemporary societies
Typical methodLong-term fieldwork and participant observationSurveys, statistics, interviews and case studies
ScaleOften one village, group or neighbourhood in depthOften large populations, regions or whole countries
Starting pointThe insider's view, then comparisonPatterns, structures and measurable trends
BranchesSocial, biological, archaeological, linguistic, appliedRural, urban, industrial, political, gender and more
Historic focusSmall-scale and non-Western societiesIndustrial societies of Europe and North America

How the two subjects grew apart

Sociology took shape in 19th century Europe as scholars tried to understand industrial cities, factories, class and the decline of older ways of life. Auguste Comte gave it its name, and Émile Durkheim, Max Weber and Karl Marx supplied its classic ideas. Its home ground was the society the scholars lived in.

Anthropology grew up at the same time but looked outward, often to societies under colonial rule. Early anthropologists studied communities in Africa, the Pacific, the Americas and South Asia, and the subject long carried the assumption that it studied other people. That assumption is now widely criticised. Anthropologists today study corporations, hospitals, laboratories and cities in their own countries, and sociologists study villages. The old division of labour has largely broken down, though the habits of method remain.

Where they meet: India as a special case

In India the two subjects have always been close. Many of the founders of Indian sociology trained in social anthropology and did village fieldwork. M. N. Srinivas, who studied the village of Rampura in Karnataka and coined the term Sanskritisation, is claimed by both disciplines. G. S. Ghurye, often called the father of Indian sociology, wrote on caste, tribe and culture in ways an anthropologist would recognise. Many Indian universities still have joint departments or shared syllabuses.

A useful rule of thumb in India is this: anthropology departments cover prehistory, human biology and tribal communities in more depth, while sociology departments cover urbanisation, social movements, stratification, demography and policy in more depth. Both study caste, kinship, religion and village life.

Which one should you study?

Choose anthropology if you are drawn to fieldwork, human evolution, archaeology, language, museums or the detailed study of particular communities. Choose sociology if you prefer large-scale social questions, policy, statistics and contemporary institutions. If you are unsure, try a short taste of each. A practical session such as an oral history and neighbourhood memory lab shows what anthropological listening feels like, while a survey project in your college shows the sociological approach.

For civil services candidates, both are offered as optional subjects. Anthropology is often chosen because its syllabus is compact and well defined, while sociology overlaps more with general studies. Read our guide to the anthropology optional for UPSC for detail on the two papers.

Seeing the difference in a museum

Museums make the contrast easy to see. An ethnographic museum such as the Bhopal Tribal Museum presents objects, homes, rituals and art in the context of the communities that made them, which is an anthropological way of seeing. A sociologist visiting the same museum might ask different questions: who funds it, who visits, and how the state represents tribal communities to the public. Asking both sets of questions in one visit is a good exercise for students of either subject.

Questions people ask

What is the main difference between anthropology and sociology?

Anthropology studies humans as a whole across time, including biology, prehistory and language, and relies mainly on long-term fieldwork in one community. Sociology studies modern society and its institutions and often uses surveys and statistics. The topics overlap, but the scope and preferred methods differ.

Is anthropology harder than sociology?

Neither is harder in general. Anthropology includes some biology and prehistory, which suits students comfortable with science. Sociology involves more theory about modern society and often more statistics. The better choice is the one whose questions interest you, since both require wide reading and clear writing.

Can I study anthropology after a sociology degree?

Yes. Many universities in India accept graduates from sociology and other social sciences for MA anthropology programmes, sometimes through an entrance test. Check the eligibility rules in each university's current admission notice, since some MSc programmes ask for a science background.

Who is the father of Indian sociology and anthropology?

G. S. Ghurye is often called the father of Indian sociology. Sarat Chandra Roy is often called the father of Indian anthropology for his studies of the Munda and Oraon and for founding the journal Man in India. M. N. Srinivas is claimed by both subjects.
